analysis.one_liner: Requires defense contractors to give the military the parts, tools, and information to repair its own equipment.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a floor vote before the 118th Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend U.S. law so that every defense contract includes a written guarantee that the government gets "fair and reasonable access" to the parts, tools, and technical information needed to diagnose, maintain, and repair what it buys — at prices no worse than what the manufacturer gives its own authorized repair shops [S2]. It would also require acquisition strategies to include at least three cost-saving proposals, require the Pentagon to report on the cost-effectiveness of its intellectual property strategy, and require members of the armed forces to log every time contractor restrictions forced them to send equipment back to the manufacturer or scrap it, with annual public reports on those "right-to-repair obstructions" [S2]. The bill never received any action in the Senate Armed Services Committee before Congress ended [S4].
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers, who currently pay contractors premium prices and long service delays when military equipment breaks and the government is locked out of fixing what it owns. Members of the armed forces — the bill is named for them — would get a formal way to log and expose every repair obstruction, and DoD readiness improves when troops can fix gear on the spot. Civilian consumers benefit indirectly: DoD is the largest single buyer of equipment in the country, and a firm legal precedent for right-to-repair in defense procurement would strengthen the broader repair-rights movement affecting consumer products.

how_it_helps.text: Every new defense contract would have to include a written promise that the contractor gives the government 'fair and reasonable access' to the parts, tools, and information used to diagnose, maintain, and repair the equipment, at prices no worse than those offered to authorized repair shops.

Acquisition strategies would have to include at least three cost-saving proposals, with the savings allowed to come from lifecycle operating and support costs but not from buying less equipment or accepting lower availability.

Soldiers, sailors, airmen, and marines who maintain equipment would have to log every instance where contractor restrictions forced them to wait for a contractor visit, ship equipment back to the manufacturer, or scrap equipment they could have repaired — and the Pentagon would have to publish an annual public report summarizing those obstructions.

Government accountability offices would audit compliance: the Comptroller General would report on contractor access within one year and on overall compliance every two years, and the Pentagon would have to publish a report on the cost-effectiveness of its intellectual property strategy.

analysis.who_pays: Defense contractors — weapons manufacturers and their service divisions — who would no longer be able to charge premium prices for service contracts and proprietary repair work on equipment the government already owns.

drawbacks.text: The bill reaches into intellectual property rights: contractors would have to give the government access to proprietary repair information, which the defense industry has long argued could undermine the business case for investing in new designs and could raise disputes over who owns the know-how.

The cost-savings requirements are projections, not guarantees — the bill requires estimates of what would be saved and how likely the savings are, and enforcement mostly takes the form of reports and compliance assessments by the Comptroller General rather than direct penalties.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main cost falls on defense contractors, who could no longer charge premium prices for service contracts and proprietary parts, and who might see lower contractor-provided service revenue. An honest supporter would acknowledge that requiring contractors to share parts, tools, and information could raise real disputes over intellectual property and, in rare cases, trade sensitive design details, and that contractors argue forced access to repair materials could weaken their incentive to invest in new technology. The bill tries to manage this by guaranteeing contractors the same prices they offer authorized repair shops, and by letting the government set terms only where no authorized channel exists. On balance the potential taxpayer savings and military readiness gains outweigh these risks, but the savings were projected, not proven, and the bill never got a committee hearing or a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on December 12, 2024 and referred to the Senate Armed Services Committee, where it stayed with no hearing, no markup, and no vote before the two-year session of Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

narrative.text: Senator Warren introduced the bill on December 12, 2024, the same day it was read twice and referred to the Senate Armed Services Committee.
The action history shows no further steps: the bill received no hearing, no committee vote, and was never brought to the Senate floor before Congress ended on January 3, 2025.
The bill attracted no cosponsors in the roughly three weeks it was alive.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Defense contractors keep the existing arrangement in which the military must often rely on them — at contractor-set prices — to service and repair the equipment the Pentagon already owns.

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and got it referred to the Senate Armed Services Committee.

against.name: Defense contractor lobby
against.role: Defense industry associations and major defense manufacturers
against.what_they_did: Defense contractors have long opposed government right-to-repair mandates as a threat to service-contract revenue and intellectual property, and right-to-repair bills consistently stall in the Armed Services committees where such objections carry weight.

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, and never drew a recorded vote, so no partisan split can be measured.

industries.note: The bill would end a lucrative business model: locking the government out of repairing its own equipment so that service work must flow back through the manufacturer at the manufacturer's price. It would require contractors to sell parts, tools, and information to the Pentagon at no worse than their best authorized-repair prices. This is why the measure matters to taxpayers — the alternative to taxpayer mechanics is contractor invoices.

industries.industry: Third-party repair providers and authorized repair shops
industries.note: The bill channels repair access through 'authorized contractors' working for the government, which could open repair work to firms other than the original manufacturer, though the primary beneficiary is meant to be military maintenance units themselves.
